div.p: In real-time systems, Functional Reactive Programming (FRP) is already playing an important role and will potentially be more so in the future. Priority-based (preemptive) FRP (P-FRP), a variant of FRP with more real-time characteristics, demands more research in its scheduling and timing analysis. Its Abort-and-Restart (AR) nature indicates that reducing preemptions can be critical for improving system performance. In this paper, we present a new non-work-conserving scheduling model, P-FRP Deferred Start (DS) model, to reduce certain preemptions under fixed priority scheduling. We analyze some properties of the P-FRP DS model. Experiments show the domination on schedulability rate and task response time to those of the P-FRP AR model. The schedulability rate increases up to 243.1% and the portion of task sets that have response time decreased ranges from 15.49% for 3-task sets to 98.28% for 10-task sets.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: In real-time systems, the correctness of a program is measured by its logical output as well as its ability to complete within certain time limits. FRP (Functional Reactive Programming) [31] is demonstrated to be effective in modeling and building real-time reactive systems such as graphics, robotic and vision applications. However, a significant feature of realtime systems, priority, is not considered in FRP. To address this problem, the P-FRP (Priority-based FPR) [21] model has been proposed as a variant of the FRP model. P-FRP maintains both the type-safety and the state-less execution paradigm of FRP, and supports priorities assigned to different tasks while not requiring the use of synchronization mechanisms between tasks in the system. It has the potential to transform the building of more and more complicated Cyber Physical Systems (CPSs), for example, in building controllers in automobile anti-lock brake systems [11].

In classic preemptive scheduling [25], a preempted task pauses execution, and resumes from where it paused (Fig. 1(a)). In order to maintain the state-less paradigm of the FRP model, unlike the classic preemptive model, P-FRP uses an Abort-and-Restart (AR, Fig. 1(b)) semantics where if a lower priority task is interrupted by a higher priority task, it has to restart from the beginning when it is resumed. Thus the P-FRP model is also called the P-FRP (fully) AR model, or simply shortened as the AR model. This provides a scheduling and programming model where response times of different tasks can be tweaked by the programmer without affecting the semantic soundness of the program.

div.p: It is obvious that the restarting in the AR model wastes the executed time (we call it the abort cost) and therefore the schedulability would benefit from reducing the number of preemptions (aborts). Our contributions in this paper include:

div.head: B. Organization
div.p: The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section II introduces the basic concepts and notations used in this paper. Section III gives a brief overview on related works. Section IV presents the DS model and some of its properties. Section V provides the experiments and results analysis, and Section VI concludes the paper.

div.head: II. BASIC CONCEPTS AND NOTATIONS
div.p: In this section, we introduce some basic concepts and notations used in the paper. We consider a hard real-time uni-processor system in the preemptive P-FRP model with n independent tasks Γ n = {τ 1 , τ 2 , ..., τ n } such that each has a constrained deadline under fixed priority scheduling. The startup of the system is assumed to be at the absolute time 0. The cost of preemption is assumed to be zero, and once a job starts to execute it will not suspend itself.

For notational convenience, we label the tasks to indicate that task τ i is assigned a unique fixed priority i (1 ≤ i ≤ n), where 1 is the highest priority and n is the lowest. An instance or invocation of a task is called a job. τ i,j refers to the j th job of τ i . Each periodic task τ i is characterized by a (maximum) computation time C i , a constant arrival time period T i between two successive jobs of the task, a relative deadline

Utilization of each task is U i = C i /T i , and the total utilization of the task set is U = n i=1 U i . Without loss of generality, we assume that all temporal parameters are assumed to be non-negative integer values.

The response time R i,j of the j th job of a task τ i is the time between the release of a job and its completion. The response time R i of a task τ i at a given release offset pattern is the maximum one of all R i,j . The Worst-Case Response Time (WCRT) of a task is derived under the worst-case release pattern that leads to the largest interference on the considered task. Such a particular scenario is often referred to as the critical instant [25] scenario.

A feasibility interval is the time interval [t, t + H) such that if all tasks are schedulable in [t, t + H) then the tasks will also be schedulable in the time interval [0, Z) : Z → ∞ [23] [2]. Here [t, t + H) is the collection of integers greater than or equal to t and less than t + H. A schedulability testing interval [a, b) is the time interval in which the schedulability of a given task set is checked. In general, the length of [a, b) is not less than that of [t, t + H).

In scheduling theory, a non-work-conserving scheduling is the one that may let the CPU be idle even when there are tasks ready for execution, while work-conserving does not. (Fully) preemptive scheduling allows a running task to be interrupted whenever a higher priority task releases, while (fully) non-preemptive scheduling does not allow a running task to be interrupted by other tasks for any reason. There are scheduling algorithms that lay in between (fully) preemptive and non-preemptive scheduling algorithms. For example, they set portions of a task preemptive and the rest non-preemptive.

div.head: III. RELATED WORK
div.p: In the classic preemptive model using RM (Rate Monotonic) scheduling for periodic tasks with deadlines equal to periods (implicit deadlines) [25], an n-task set is schedulable if the first instance of each task can finish within its deadline when these tasks are released at the same time (synchronous release). RM is optimal among other existing fixed priority scheduling algorithms for implicit-deadline tasks [25]. When deadline is less than period, Deadline Monotonic (DM) uses deadlines instead of periods and is similar to RM [8]. For arbitrary deadline task-sets with potentially some tasks having deadlines greater than periods, both the RM and the DM schemes are not optimal [22]. There are extensive analysis of schedulability for the tasks with given priority assignments under the classic preemptive model [8], [14] in decades.

However, these results do not apply directly to the P-FRP model due to the abort-and-restart semantics of P-FRP systems. RM is not optimal in the P-FRP AR model [5] and it is even unknown whether there exists an optimal one other than exhaustive tests over all possible priority assignments. In [19], [20] the authors presented their feasibility intervals and schedulability analysis for the AR model of the P-FRP systems. The authors of [32] studied some other priority assignment algorithms and they confirmed that none of those algorithms is optimal in the AR model. Readers are referred to [35] for a brief survey on the P-FRP task scheduling.

In alternatives of the AR model, real-time Java is designed to allow programmers to develop a real-time application using the Java language. The example of Preemptible Atomic Regions (PAR) was introduced for real-time Java [26]. This is a new concurrency control abstraction for real-time systems. The basic notions of the AR model and the PAR model are similar but PAR makes a log of the shared resource and then the state of the resource will be rolled back if the task is preempted. The authors of [33] proposed the Deferred Abort (DA) model where a task is divided into two regions: the first region is preemptive (i.e., AR) and the second region is non-preemptive and nonabortable. It works in the preemptive region in the same way as the AR model does, and works in the non-preemptive region in the same way as the classic non-preemptive model does. The DA model aims to reduce the number of preemptions by eliminating some preemptions and can be regarded as a nonfully-AR model. Notice that the deferred preemption has been studied in the classic preemptive model, such as [7], [13], [10], and the deferred abort can be viewed as an application of the deferred preemption in the P-FRP model. Preliminary research of the DS model was presented in [34].

The most effective way to reduce preemption cost is to disable preemptions completely, which means a non-preemptive scheduling. In most non-preemptive schedulings, however, a task can experience blocking from other tasks. A careful arrangement of task execution can avoid the blocking, while it most likely works in a non-work-conserving way. The schedulability conditions in non-preemptive scheduling are NP-hard in the strong sense as shown in [18], and in the same paper, the authors presented also an exact (necessary and sufficient) test for schedulability of non-preemptive Earliest Deadline First (npEDF) for periodic tasks with arbitrary release offsets. A comprehensive schedulability analysis of non-preemptive systems was performed in [17]. Sufficient conditions for the schedulability of periodic (and sporadic) tasks scheduled by non-preemptive RM (npRM) have been studied [17], [1], [30]. Clairvoyant EDF (cEDF) [16] and group-based EDF (gEDF) [24] are two heuristic algorithms for this NP-hard problem.

Since the problem is NP-hard, special cases were studied, such as harmonic task sets [15], [12], [29]. It should be stated that in [29] the Precautious-RM algorithm was proposed and it was an O(1) fixed priority based algorithm which can be used in many more cases [27], [28], for example, the Efficient Precautious-RM (EP-RM) [27] as non-preemptive scheduling algorithms under RM priority assignment for less restricted harmonic task sets where the periods of tasks are an integer multiple of the shortest task period. The schedulability of the non-preemptive recurring task model were analyzed in [4]. The authors of [9] used the non-preemptive task model to reduce jitter. Preemption normally works well to meet timing requirement in real-time system design; however, in many cases, a fully preemptive scheduler produces many unnecessary preemptions. To reduce the runtime overhead due to preemptions and still preserve the schedulability of the task set, limited preemption has been investigated [3], [10].

div.head: IV. DEFERRED START OF P-FRP
div.p: We introduce the DS model for the P-FRP systems in this section. We first give the definition and several properties of the DS model, then present feasibility interval analysis for this new model.

div.head: A. The Model
div.p: We know that there are executed but incomplete execution regions for an individual task in both the classic preemptive model and the P-FRP AR model (including the DA model). The difference is that in the classic preemptive model the already-executed part of the task does not need to re-execute, i.e., the executed but incomplete execution regions of the same task are valid towards the complete execution of the task, while those in the P-FRP AR model are not. In fact, in the P-FRP model an executed but incomplete execution region has no contribution to and effect on the completion of a P-FRP task. So the DS model can be derived from the AR model: in the DS model (DS scheduling) a task is scheduled as if it was in the AR model with the condition that it is scheduled to start executing only when there is enough time to finish its execution. As a result, the number of preemptions in DS scheduling decreases to zero, which makes it seem to be a non-preemptive non-work-conserving scheduling. It differs, however, from existing classic nonpreemptive scheduling algorithms in that:

1) though each successfully scheduled task occupies a continuous block of time at the length of the task's execution time in both the classic non-preemptive scheduling and the DS scheduling, the completion time, hence the response time, of a higher-priority task in DS scheduling is not affected by tasks with lower priorities. A task yields the processor only when it is preempted by higher-priority tasks and this would make the incomplete execution useless according to the P-FRP semantics, and not because of the arrival of lower-priority 2) in the DS model it keeps strictly the order of priorities as in the classic preemptive model and the P-FRP AR model, so the DS model is not comparable to those classic nonpreemptive models that allow a task delay execution while it should start instantly.
3) in the DS model there is no non-preemptive region as that in the DA model and some classic non-preemptive models.

By shifting from work-conserving to non-work-conserving, compared to the AR model, in the DS model, (1) there is no waste of execution time; (2) due to that a higher-priority task yields the processor when it will not finish execution in some time intervals, a lower-priority task has higher chance to be scheduled earlier and successfully for execution, thus the schedulability rate of task sets may increase, and the response times of individual tasks may decrease.

Table I shows where the DS model is in the context of preemptive P-FRP. Both the existing AR and DA models are work-conserving, and to the best of our knowledge, the DS model is the first non-work-conserving model proposed for P-FRP systems.
The DS model presented in this paper is based on fully AR, leaving the treatment of variations of the DS model which are neither fully preemptive nor fully non-preemptive as an open problem.

div.head: B. Properties
div.p: We present several properties of the DS model in this subsection.

div.head: Theorem 1. In P-FRP systems, if a task set is schedulable in the AR model, it is also schedulable in the DS model.
div.p: Proof: The proof is conducted using an inductive method for a Γ n task system, Base: For n = 1, where there is only task τ 1 , it is obvious that both schedulings are the same, thus if it is schedulable in the AR model then it is schedulable in the DS model.
Inductive hypothesis: For n = k, suppose that if Γ k is schedulable in the AR model, then it is also schedulable in the DS model.

Inductive step: When n = k + 1, i.e., Γ k+1 = Γ k ∪ {τ k+1 }, the aim of this step is to prove that if Γ k+1 is schedulable in the AR model, then it is also schedulable in the DS model. Without loss of generality, we can assume the newly added task in Γ k+1 is τ k+1 ; otherwise, we can still assume that the Γ k consists of the first k highest priority tasks and by the inductive hypothesis, this Γ k is schedulable in both the AR and the DS models. Notice also that adding a task with the lowest priority does not change the schedulability of the existing task set according to the definition of the AR and the DS models.
For Γ k+1 = Γ k ∪ {τ k+1 } which is schedulable in the AR model, by inductive hypothesis, Γ k is schedulable in the DS model, and now we need to prove τ k+1 is schedulable in the DS model.

It is noted that, for the same task set Γ k+1 , for each job of each task, its release time point is the same in both the AR model and the DS model, and a lower priority task has no effect on the schedule of higher priority tasks. For any job τ k+1,j (j ≥ 1) of the task τ k+1 , since τ k+1 is schedulable in the AR model, suppose that the release time point of job τ k+1,j is t r and the completion time point is t c . Given the schedule S DS of Γ k in the DS model and there are m (m ≥ 0) unoccupied time intervals in the schedule S DS between the time point t r and the time point t c -C k+1 that have length no shorter than C k+1 . If m = 0, the finish time of job τ k+1,j in the DS model is the same as that in the AR model. If m > 0, job τ k+1,j is scheduled successfully at a time point in the DS model ahead of that in the AR model. The theorem is then proved.

Lemma 1. In P-FRP systems, if a task set is schedulable in the DS model under a given priority assignment, there is no guarantee that it is schedulable in the AR model under the same priority assignment.

Proof: We use an example to show this property. Consider a synchronously released task set Γ 3 = {τ 1 , τ 2 , τ 3 } with implicit deadlines where C 1 = 1, T 1 = 5; C 2 = 2, T 2 = 4; C 3 = 2, T 3 = 10, and the subindex indicates the priority.
Simply referring to the Figs.1(b) and (c), it is clear that Γ 3 is schedulable in the DS model, but the first job of τ 3 will miss its deadline in the AR model.

Theorem 1 together with Lemma 1 imply that a sufficient test for a task set in the DS model is that it is schedulable in the AR model. Moreover, an AR model's sufficient or exact schedulability test is also a sufficient test for the DS model.
From the definition and analysis of the DS model, we also have Lemma 2.

div.head: Lemma 2. Compared to the AR model, the DS model may reduce the response time of a lower priority task without delaying the completion of higher priority tasks, and hence it may decrease the response time of all tasks except the two highest priority ones.
div.p: Proof: For a task system Γ n of 1 ≤ n ≤ 2, tasks' response time in the DS model are the same as those in the AR model (see the analysis on τ 1 and τ 2 below).
When n ≥ 3, according to the scheduling rules of the DS model, we have that:
1) τ 1 , the task with the highest priority, is scheduled right at the time when it is released, and its response time is hence exactly its execution time C 1 .

2) After τ 1 is scheduled, τ 2 is selected. For a certain job of τ 2 , in the AR model, before it finally finishes execution at time t, it might have been aborted k (k > 0) times, hence wasting k time intervals, [t 1 , t 2 ), [t 3 , t 4 ), ..., [t 2k+1 , t 2k+2 ). On the other hand, when it is scheduled in the DS model, its completion time is still t since none of the k time intervals is long enough and the DS scheduler simply skips them. So the response time of τ 2 in both models is the same, except that k time intervals are idle in the DS model. If there is no abort, we apply the same reasoning to τ 3 .

3) After τ 2 is scheduled, τ 3 is selected. In the DS model, jobs of τ 3 may be able to use the time intervals which are wasted in the AR model and saved in the DS model after scheduling jobs of τ 2 . Even though τ 3 may not be able to benefit in shortening its response time from the saving intervals resulting from scheduling τ 2 , it does not suffer lengthening of its response time. Besides, the time intervals that are not used by τ 3 may also be used in scheduling other lower priority tasks.

4) For τ 4 and others, similar reasoning as in 3) applies. Hence Lemma 2 is proved. Theorem 1, Lemma 1, and Lemma 2 show that if a task set is schedulable in the AR model it is also schedulable in the DS model, and some of the task sets that are not schedulable in the AR model can be schedulable in the DS model. Also, for a task set schedulable in both the AR and the DS models, its response time in the DS model is not longer than that in the AR model. Thus the DS model dominates the AR model in terms of task schedulability and response time.

div.head: C. Feasibility Interval Analysis
div.p: We give a concept first. In the DS model, when there is an available time interval but a task is not able to use it because of its short length, we say that the task is interfered by higherpriority tasks. Lemma 3. In the DS model for P-FRP systems, the ratemonotonic priority assignment is not an optimal priority assignment with synchronous release of tasks.
Proof: If there is a P-FRP task set in the DS model which is unschedulable by the RM priority assignment but is schedulable by another priority assignment, this lemma is then proved.

Consider a 2-task system Γ 2 : C 1 = 7, T 1 = 15, C 2 = 3, T 2 = 12 that released synchronously at time 0, as shown in Fig. 2. Using the same method shown in Fig. 1, in the time interval of [0, 60), the third job of τ 1 finishes at time point 46 which is 1 time unit later than its deadline when using the RM priority assignment (Fig. 2(a)). After exchange their priority, both tasks are scheduled successfully (Fig. 2(b)).

In fact, there is still no known priority assignment or release pattern to form the critical instant of the P-FRP DS model. Therefore, efficient feasibility interval analysis and schedulability test algorithms and implementations for a given release pattern are demanded before finding the WCRT of an n-task system.

When a given phasing of Γ n satisfying 0 ≤ Φ k < T k for all k, 1 ≤ k ≤ n, we designate the given phasing with a term of the basic phasing condition [19]. When Γ n satisfies the basic phasing condition, each Γ k (1 ≤ k ≤ n) also satisfies this condition. The term of the Initial Busy Condition remains the same as that in the AR model [19]. Definition 1. For Γ n under fixed priority scheduling, the Initial Busy Condition for a given priority assignment refers to the condition: For each i, 2 ≤ i ≤ n, min 1≤j<i {Φ j } < Φ i + C i and Φ i ≤ max 1≤j<i {Φ j + R j,1 } where R j,1 is the response time of the first job of task τ j for the same given priority assignment [19].

div.head: V. EXPERIMENTS AND RESULTS ANALYSIS A. Experiment Setup
div.p: The experiments are conducted on a desktop computer with a CPU of i3-4130 3.4GHz, 8 GB memory and Ubuntu 14.04.3 LTS 64-bit Desktop operating system. The objective is to deliver comparisons between the AR model and the DS model on the schedulable rate increasing for task sets and the response times decreasing for individual tasks that achieved in the DS model.

From the discussion above, the DS scheduling can be viewed as a kind of non-preemptive scheduling. Therefore, it shares the same limitation with non-preemptive scheduling in that the utilization factor of an infeasible task set can be close to 0 [28]. Hence the utilization factor itself of task sets in the experiments is not our concern. We choose a utilization factor that is neither very high nor very low. And with this chosen utilization factor, we should have enough number of schedulable task sets as well as that of non-schedulable task sets in the AR model for the purpose of comparison. In our experiment, only necessary condition of U ≤ 1 is considered. As we have stated in above sections, the difference between the AR model and the DS model with n-task system Γ n where n = 1, 2 is trivial. So our experiments start from 3task sets. The task sets we generate have 3, 4, ..., 10 tasks respectively. For each group, we generate 5000 task sets. The periods T k are randomly generated in range [15,70] and deadlines are set to the corresponding periods. Note that the period range is not of significance to our comparison objective. Release offsets are randomly set to 0 or 1 satisfying the initial busy condition (see Definition 1). The total utilization factor of a task set is set to 0.6. We use the UUniFast algorithm [6] to generate n (n = 3, 4, .., 10) utilization factors U k (1 ≤ k ≤ n) in a descending order such that the total utilization factor U = n k=1 U k equals to the given value, 0.6, in this experiment. We then shuffle those U k to a random order for the consideration of generalization. The computation time of each task is computed by C k = U k × T k , and set C k = 1 if it is 0 after this computation.

div.head: B. Acceptance Ratio
div.p: Acceptance ratio means the proportion of the number of task sets deemed to be schedulable by a test method to the total number of task sets tested. Numbers of schedulable task sets in our experiments are listed in Fig. 3. The rows of AR and DS are the numbers of schedulable task sets in the AR and the DS model respectively. In the third row, Rate is calculated by (DS -AR)/AR × 100(%), and for better visualization, we multiply the value of Rate by 10 in the figure . We can see that the numbers of schedulable task sets in the DS model dominate those in the AR model, and the DS model has 12.0%, 42.5%, 79.3%, 104.34%, 154.1%, 191.5%, 230.9%, 243.1% more schedulable tasks. In this experiment, the improvement of the acceptance ratio increases along with the increasing of the tasks number in a task set. The reason is that with more tasks in a task set, the potentially wasted time increases in the AR model, and hence the acceptance ratio of a task system benefits more from applying the DS model.

div.head: C. Response Time
div.p: Experimental results confirm that scheduling tasks in the DS model has no task response time increase compared to that in the AR model. We list statistics of the response time changes of task sets in our experiment. From Table II, Γ 3 has 2246 schedulable task sets in both the AR and the DS model, and 348 (15.49%) of them have response time decreased. As of Γ 10 , 57 out of 58 (98.28%) have response time decreased. The portion of task sets that have response time decreased ranges from 15.49% to 98.28%, and the number increases as the number of tasks in a task set increases. The reason is that more tasks in a task set leads to more interfering cost for lower-priority tasks in the AR model.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
div.p: We have proposed our research on Deferred Start (DS), a new alternative model for preemptive P-FRP systems. We have presented several properties, and also analyzed the feasibility interval problem of the DS model. Analysis and experiments show that the DS model increases the schedulability rate and decreases the response times of P-FRP tasks compared to the AR model. Similar to the AR model there is also no known critical instant for the new DS model.

Moreover, from the generalized analysis we have presented in this paper, considering the fact that the DS model scheduling is a type of non-preemptive scheduling, more restricted cases such as those with task sets consisting of harmonic periods and with widely distributed periods worth further study.

We propose a new model, the P-FRP Deferred Start (DS) model, or shortened as the DS model, for P-FRP systems. The DS model (see Fig.1(c)) reduces the number of preemptions by postponing the starting of a job, and thus it is a non-work-conserving model. 2) We present the schedulability and response time analysis for the DS model. Experiments and analysis indicate that the DS model has equivalent or better schedulability and response time performance compared to that of the AR model, which is not true in any other known non-work-conserving models.
